newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs welcome EU summit deal as good compromise.
newsitem.headline: Czechs welcome EU summit deal as good compromise.

text.p: The Czech Republic welcomed on Wednesday the outcome of the European Union's Amsterdam summit as a good compromise and said it would do all it could to remain a leading candidate for EU membership.
The foreign ministry said in a statement it saw the result of the summit, and the Intergovernmental Conference (IGC), as a good basis for starting the process of EU enlargement.
"The results of the EU summit are a good compromise which move forward the question of European integration by another important step," the statement said.
The Czech Republic, along with Poland and Hungary, are widely seen as the frontrunners for EU membership.
The summit was supposed to resolve issues, particularly on majority voting, so that the 15 current members could begin talks on joining the EU with leading candidates in six months.
The ministry said it was aware of the increased pressure on the preparation of candidates for membership.

"The Czech foreign ministry is prepared to expend maximum effort so that the Czech Republic should continue to be one of the leading candidates for membership of the European Union," the statement said.
However, other officials and analysts were not as content with the less than decisive outcome of the summit.

Daniel Kroupa, chairman of the Czech parliament's delegation for cooperation with the European Parliament, was quoted by the CTK news agency as saying that the outcome was "very bad news" which would mean the Czech Republic would have to pay greater attention to the negotiations on EU accession.
Earlier, Jiri Sedivy, deputy head of Prague's Institute of International Relations, said the difficulty in reaching a deal in Amsterdam did not bode well for the accession talks.
"Explicitly, there is no change vis-a-vis enlargement, but implicitly the very proceedings of the summit indicate it is going to be more difficult than we expected," Sedivy said.
He did not expect the Czech Republic, or other leading contenders, to be admitted before 2005 at the earliest.
